language_wrapper: Consider a cyclic sequence of {alpha} real numbers a_1, a_2, ..., a_{alpha}. Fix a step size {step} with 1 <= {step} < {alpha}, and interpret indices modulo {alpha}. Define the set of pair-sums S_{step} = { |a_i + a_{i+{step}}| : i = 1, 2, ..., {alpha} }. Determine the smallest positive integer t such that for every choice of the reals a_1, ..., a_{alpha}, the inequality max_{1 <= i <= {alpha}} |a_i| <= t * max S_{step} always holds.
hardness_rationale: This family generalizes the seed from adjacent (step-1) pair-sums on a single odd cycle to pair-sums with an arbitrary step on the cyclic index, which decomposes the index set into gcd(alpha, step) disjoint cycles. Solving it requires identifying the induced cycle length m = alpha / gcd(alpha, step), proving that a uniform inequality holds if and only if m is odd, and constructing both an exact linear identity (upper bound) and a sharp extremal assignment via recurrence along the cycle (lower bound). The solution leverages modular arithmetic, cycle decomposition, and a duality-style argument for the operator induced by the pair-sum map, which is conceptually and technically more advanced than the seed’s single-cycle telescoping.
notes:
Proof of correctness: Let n = alpha and d = step. Partition indices 1..n into cycles under the map i -> i + d (mod n); there are g = gcd(n, d) cycles, each of length m = n/g. Focus on a single cycle C = (v_0, v_1, ..., v_{m-1}) where v_k = v_0 + k d (mod n), and define b_k := a_{v_k} + a_{v_{k+1}} (indices mod m along the cycle). If m is even, the alternating assignment a_{v_k} = (-1)^k yields b_k = 0 for all k, so max |a_i| cannot be bounded by any finite multiple of max |b_k|; thus the inequality fails for any finite t. Hence we require m odd.
Upper bound (existence of finite t when m is odd): Define coefficients c_k = (1/2)(-1)^k for k=0..m-1. Then \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} c_k b_k = \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} (1/2)(-1)^k (a_{v_k} + a_{v_{k+1}}) = \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} (1/2)((-1)^k a_{v_k} + (-1)^k a_{v_{k+1}}). Reindex the second sum: \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} (1/2)(-1)^k a_{v_{k+1}} = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} (1/2)(-1)^{j-1} a_{v_j}. Adding the two parts, every a_{v_j} has coefficient (1/2)((-1)^j + (-1)^{j-1}) = 0 except for j=0, where wrap-around contributes an extra term yielding coefficient (1/2)((-1)^0 + (-1)^{m-1}) = (1/2)(1 + 1) = 1 since m is odd. Thus \sum_k c_k b_k = a_{v_0}. Therefore for any index i, |a_i| <= \sum_k |c_k| |b_k| <= (m/2) max_k |b_k|. Taking the maximum over all indices yields max_i |a_i| <= (m/2) max_i |a_i + a_{i+d}|. Hence any integer t >= ceil(m/2) works.
Lower bound (sharpness): Fix the cycle C and prescribe b_k = (-1)^k for k=0..m-1 (so max |b_k| = 1). The recurrence a_{v_{k+1}} = b_k - a_{v_k} determines a unique sequence along C. After traversing the cycle (m steps), consistency requires a_{v_0} = a_{v_m} = (-1)^m a_{v_0} + \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} (-1)^j b_j. Since m is odd, (-1)^m = -1, so 2 a_{v_0} = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} (-1)^j b_j = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} 1 = m, giving a_{v_0} = m/2. Consequently, max_i |a_i| >= m/2 while max_i |a_i + a_{i+d}| = 1. This shows that no integer t < ceil(m/2) can satisfy the inequality for all sequences. Combining both bounds, the smallest positive integer t is ceil(m/2).
General instance validity: The verifier ensures m is odd and at least 5 to avoid trivialities and impossibilities. The answer is computed as (m+1)//2, which matches the proven minimal integer bound.
Relation to the seed: The seed corresponds to d=1 on a single cycle of length n (which must be odd), yielding t = ceil(n/2). The generalized family introduces an arbitrary step d, requiring analysis of gcd(n, d) and cycle decomposition, and uses the same core logical idea (alternating telescoping along an odd cycle) with a more intricate structure.
source_question: Find the smallest positive integer \(t\), such that for any real numbers \(a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_{4467}\), the inequality \(\max(|a_1|, |a_2|, \cdots, |a_{4467}|) \leq t \cdot \max(|a_1 + a_2|, |a_2 + a_3|, \cdots, |a_{4466} + a_{4467}|, |a_{4467} + a_1|)\) always hold true.
